title: Face Vomiting Emoji 🤮: When “Ew” Isn't Strong Enough
description: 🤮 shows a face throwing up. It means you are violently ill or completely repulsed by something. See how people use it for disgust, cringe and hangovers.
summary: The 🤮 face vomiting emoji means the sender is throwing up or wants to. Literally it covers stomach bugs, food poisoning and hangovers. Figuratively it is the strongest disgust emoji available, used for anything the sender finds repulsive, from a bad smell to an opinion or a person's behavior.
meaning: There is nothing coded about 🤮. A stream of green pours from an open mouth, and the emoji means exactly that. When people use it literally they are describing a miserable night with norovirus, a reaction to bad takeout, morning sickness or the price of too many drinks. It tends to be sent after the worst has happened, as a report.

As a reaction it expresses total rejection. A friend shares a screenshot of an ex's cheesy post, a news story about a restaurant's kitchen or a food combination from the internet, and 🤮 is the verdict. It is cruder and more final than the green nauseated face. The message is not that the thing is unpleasant but that the sender's body refuses it.

A lot of the time the disgust is theatrical. Teenagers send it to siblings, friends send it about each other's taste in music, and single people post it under engagement announcements as an obvious joke. The exaggeration is the humor. Tone depends on the relationship: the same emoji that is funny between best friends is hostile from a stranger.

It is also used in pile-ons, where many accounts flood a post or a person with 🤮. In that setting it works as public shaming, and the sheer repetition is the point. Aimed at an individual's appearance, identity or relationship, it is one of the more aggressive things an emoji can say, and platforms sometimes treat it as harassment.

contexts.label: In texting
contexts.body: Friends use it as a punchline to gross stories and as a status report during illness. A row of them, 🤮🤮🤮, usually means either a truly awful stomach bug or disgust turned up for comic effect. It is rarely ambiguous, because the topic of conversation makes the meaning clear.

contexts.label: On social media
contexts.body: It appears in reactions to unappetizing food videos, viral stories of bad dates and anything described as giving the ick. On platforms with reaction emojis it is sometimes used to register strong disapproval of a post. Brands and public figures see it when a campaign or statement lands badly.

contexts.label: About feeling ill
contexts.body: For real sickness it is graphic but efficient. Telling a manager or a host that you have been 🤮 all night ends the discussion; nobody asks you to come in anyway. Some people find it too vivid and prefer the nauseated or thermometer face for the same message.

contexts.label: At work
contexts.body: Outside of a close team joking about a truly bad lunch, it has little place in professional messages. Reacting with it to an idea, a design or a document is insulting. If you need to say you are sick, describe it in words or use a milder emoji.

examples.text: Food poisoning from that buffet 🤮 been up since 3am
examples.meaning: The sender has literally been throwing up all night.

examples.text: He chews with his mouth open AND talks 🤮
Mayo on a peanut butter sandwich?? 🤮
examples.meaning: They find the food combination revolting.
Affectionate mock disgust at a friend's happy relationship.
A hangover has ruined a particular drink for them.

combos.meaning: Nausea turning into vomiting; shows a reaction getting worse.
Spending the night in the bathroom with a stomach illness or hangover.
So disgusted or so sick that the sender is jokingly finished.
Drank far too much and paid for it.

confusedWith.difference: 🤢 is green and struggling to hold it in, so it reads as queasy or mildly grossed out. 🤮 has lost that struggle. Reach for it only when you want the maximum level of disgust.
🤬 covers its mouth with censored swearing and expresses rage. Both have something over the mouth at small sizes, but one is furious and the other is sick or revolted.
🤒 says sick in a general, sympathetic way and suits fevers and colds. 🤮 names one specific and unpleasant symptom, which makes it more vivid and less polite.

avoid: Do not aim it at a person's looks, identity, partner or cooking, where it is simply cruel.
Avoid it around people with eating disorders or a strong fear of vomiting, for whom the image can be upsetting.
Leave it out of professional feedback of any kind.
design: A face with scrunched or X-shaped eyes and raised brows, mouth wide open and releasing a stream of green vomit. All major vendors use green for the liquid. The face itself is usually yellow, though some designs tint it slightly green, and the eyes vary between tightly shut, crossed out and wide with distress.

faqs.a: It means something is disgusting to the sender: gross, cringe, repulsive or deeply unappealing. It is the emoji version of saying that makes me want to throw up. It is often exaggerated for humor rather than meant literally.

It depends on the target. About your own stomach or a shared gross-out, it is harmless. About another person, their body, their food or something they are proud of, it is rude and can be hurtful. In public comments it is usually taken as hostile.

faqs.q: What does it mean when someone replies 🤮 to my story?
faqs.a: From a close friend it is most likely teasing, especially if the story showed a couple photo or something sentimental. From someone you do not know well, they are expressing real dislike. If you are unsure, their other messages will tell you which.

faqs.q: When did the vomiting emoji come out?
faqs.a: It was approved in Unicode 10.0 and reached keyboards in 2017, a year after the green nauseated face. The same release added the exploding head, the face with monocle and the shushing face.
